# Methods {#sec-methods .deo-methods}

## Design

We conducted a narrative review of multiple cases using publicly available
documents. We chose a narrative rather than a systematic design because the
number of relevant cases is small, much of the evidence is grey literature
(reports and documents not published in journals), and the aim was to draw
lessons rather than to estimate an effect. The review was checked against
SANRA, a six-item scale for assessing the quality of narrative reviews
[@baethge2019]. No ethical approval was required because only public documents
were used.

## Definitions

A *citizen* was defined as anyone acting outside a paid research or government
role. Because this definition includes civil-society professionals who
volunteer their expertise, we recorded separately for each case whether leading
roles were held by lay members of the public, by patient-researchers, by
civil-society experts, or by institutions. The *unit of analysis* was the
citizen-data activity rather than the organisation as a whole. For example, in
a case where an organisation shared data from its service, we scored the
data-sharing programme, not the service.

## Sources

Cases were first identified through scoping searches of the web and the
reference lists of known projects. To check for missed cases, we then ran
structured searches on 4 November 2026 in PubMed, Scopus and Europe PMC (which
also indexes preprints), Google Scholar (first 200 results per query, ranked by
relevance), the Indonesian journal index Garuda, and two citizen-science
project directories (EU-Citizen.Science and SciStarter), in English and Bahasa
Indonesia. Three query sets covered citizen science in mental health,
participatory mental-health research in Indonesia, and controversies over the
use of mental-health data. Exact queries, filters, numbers of results and
screening outcomes are reported in Supplement S4, following the PRISMA-S
extension for reporting literature searches [@rethlefsen2021]. For each
included case, we then retrieved project websites, organisational reports and
the reference lists of retrieved documents. Sources were preferred in the
following order: peer-reviewed article, preprint or conference proceedings,
organisational report, project website, and news. News was used only where no
other source documented a fact, and this is noted in the text.

## Case selection

Cases were selected purposively. To be included, a case had to (1) concern
health, with priority for stress, depression, anxiety, burnout or resilience;
(2) give citizens a role beyond being data subjects in at least one stage of
research, or, for failure cases, involve data from people with mental-health
needs; (3) have documented outcomes, or be clearly identified as ongoing; and
(4) be described in at least two independent sources, at least one of which was
a peer-reviewed article, preprint or organisational report. We sought a mix of
Indonesian and international cases, of successes and failures, and of
citizen-led and institution-led projects. @tbl-cases lists the candidate cases
and the reason for including or excluding each.

## Scoring framework

Each case was scored on 18 items grouped into four domains [@tbl-scoring]. The items
were derived from three sources: the stages of the research lifecycle; Haklay's
typology of participation [@haklay2013]; and the ten principles of citizen
science of the European Citizen Science Association [@robinson2018]. Principles
1, 2 and 4 of the ECSA framework are covered by Domains A and C; the remaining
principles each map to one item in Domain B. A crosswalk between items and
source frameworks is given in Supplement S1.

Each item was scored on four levels: **●** met; **◐** partly met; **○** not
met; and **NR**, not reported. A score of ○ required evidence that the practice
did not happen; where sources were silent, the item was scored NR. This
distinction matters because the review relies on public documents, and an
unreported practice may still have taken place.

::: {#tbl-scoring .list-table}
Scoring framework (full definitions in Supplement S1)

- - Item
  - Question
  - ● Met when sources show…

- - []{colspan=3} **C. What changed because citizens took part**

- - C1
  - Citizens changed the research question
  - A focus or measure studied because citizens raised it, which researchers or officials were not studying

- - C2
  - Findings came before the official or usual route
  - Dated sources show results published before the official or conventional equivalent

- - C3
  - Findings were trusted and used
  - Documented use by a government, health service or funder

- - []{colspan=3} **A. Citizens' highest documented role at each stage**

- - A1
  - Choosing the question
  - Citizens led or co-decided

- - A2
  - Designing methods and tools
  - Citizens led or co-decided

- - A3
  - Collecting data
  - Citizens led or co-decided

- - A4
  - Analysing and interpreting data
  - Citizens led or co-decided

- - A5
  - Writing and sharing results
  - Citizens led or co-decided

- - A6
  - Acting on findings
  - Citizens led or co-decided

- - []{colspan=3} **B. How the project was run**

- - B1
  - Both citizens and science benefited (ECSA 3)
  - A stated benefit to participants and a scientific output

- - B2
  - Participants got results back (ECSA 5)
  - Results returned in a form participants could use

- - B3
  - Data and results are open (ECSA 7)
  - Both openly available, or under controlled access for sensitive data

- - B4
  - Contributions acknowledged in a form contributors chose (ECSA 8)
  - Acknowledgement, with contributors able to choose named, collective or anonymous credit

- - B5
  - Data quality checked, limitations stated (ECSA 6)
  - Both described

- - B6
  - Ethics and data protection in place (ECSA 10)
  - Ethics review and a consent or privacy approach

- - B7
  - Project evaluated itself (ECSA 9)
  - A formal evaluation published

- - []{colspan=3} **D. Durability and harm**

- - D1
  - Activity lasted, or ended as planned
  - Still running, or closed with a hand-over

- - D2
  - Volunteers and participants protected from harm
  - Risks foreseen and managed, no harm documented
:::

In Domain A, ● means citizens led or co-decided a stage, ◐ means they
contributed or were consulted, and ○ means they had no role. Each stage was
scored at the highest role documented. People who were sampled as survey
respondents or who used a service were not counted as contributing to data
collection; members of the public who enrolled themselves in an open
crowdsourcing study were counted as contributors (◐).

Two summaries were derived from the item scores rather than scored separately.
The *level of participation* followed Haklay's typology: crowdsourcing if
citizens contributed only to data collection; distributed intelligence if they
also contributed to analysis or interpretation; participatory science if they
were consulted on or contributed to the question or design; and extreme citizen
science if they led or co-decided the question. Cases in which citizens had no
research role were labelled "data subjects only". The *verdict* gave most
weight to Domain C, reflecting the review's focus on what citizen involvement
changes. A case was a **success** if findings were documented as used (C3 = ●)
and the activity lasted or ended as planned (D1 ≥ ◐); a **failure** if findings
were rejected (C3 = ○), the activity collapsed (D1 = ○), or harm was not
addressed (D2 = ○); **partial** if neither applied; and **insufficient
evidence** if C3 or D1 was not reported and no failure criterion was met. These
rules were fixed before scoring.

## Coding procedure

Two coders scored each case independently. The framework was first piloted on
two cases, after which definitions were refined; the refinements are listed in
Supplement S1. Agreement is reported as the percentage of cells on which coders
agreed [to be completed: XX%]; disagreements were resolved by discussion. Every
score is supported by a citation and a one-line justification in Supplement S2.
To limit bias arising from the lead author's role in a research platform (see
Declarations), the second coder had no ties to that platform and held the final
decision on disputed cells.

## Synthesis

For each item we counted the number of cases scored ●. Before scoring, we set
the thresholds for the summary: an item was *done well across cases* if it was
met in at least six of eight cases, and *consistently lacking* if it was met in
two or fewer. Consistently lacking items were further divided by whether the
cases mostly scored ○ (not done) or NR (not reported). We compared cases by
leadership (citizen-led versus institution-led), setting (Indonesian versus
international) and verdict (success versus failure), and drew a numbered list
of lessons, each linked to the cases that support it.
